opus-5.5.text:
I usually start by looking at what actually changed in the architecture, because that tells you most of the story. Some new generations are mostly the same skeleton: a standard transformer with more parameters, more data, and better post-training. For those, the adaptation on the serving side is fairly light. You check that the kernels still hit good utilization at the new sizes, retune the parallelism, and you're mostly done.

The harder cases are when the model changes the shape of the computation. A new attention variant, a different way of handling the KV cache, mixture-of-experts with a new routing scheme, much longer context, or multimodal inputs mixed into the token stream. Each of those touches the core of the inference engine: memory management, scheduling, batching, sometimes the kernels themselves. So the first question I ask is: does this break any assumption our system was built on? If the answer is yes, that's real engineering work, not just configuration.

The second thing I look at is the workload, not just the model. How people use a model matters as much as its weights. If a new generation is mostly used for agentic, multi-turn work with lots of shared prefixes, then things like prefix caching and structured output become much more important than raw single-request speed. Reasoning models that generate very long outputs shift the bottleneck toward decoding and memory bandwidth. So even if the architecture barely changes, the usage pattern can force you to rethink your optimizations.

In practice, we try to get a working version running correctly as fast as possible, ideally on day one, and then profile it under realistic traffic. The profiler tells you honestly where the time goes, and that's usually where you find out how much adaptation you really need, rather than guessing up front. Over time we've also tried to make the system more modular, so that when the next architectural surprise comes, and it always does, the change stays contained instead of rippling through everything.

r001.rationale: The response says generations with mostly the same architecture need light adaptation, while architectural changes that alter computation require substantial engineering work.

fable-5.1.text:
Ying Sheng: That's a good question, and honestly the answer has changed a lot over the past couple of years. When I think about adaptation, I'm really thinking about it from the inference-system side, because that's where I spend most of my time.

The first thing I look at is the architecture. If a new model is basically a dense transformer with the same attention pattern we've seen before, the adaptation is pretty small. Maybe you need to support a new tokenizer, a new position encoding, some small tweaks to normalization. That's a few days of work for an engine like SGLang, and most of the time goes into verification rather than writing code.

But the moment the architecture does something structurally different, the cost jumps. Mixture-of-experts is a good example. Suddenly you need expert-parallel routing, load balancing across GPUs, different memory layouts. Or when models started using very long contexts, the KV cache became the bottleneck, and we had to rethink how we allocate and share memory. Multimodal inputs are another one, because now the pipeline has image encoders, different batching behavior, and the scheduler has to understand all of that.

The second thing I look at is what the model is used for, not just what it is. A model built for agentic workloads with lots of tool calls and structured outputs puts different stress on the system than a chatbot. You care much more about prefix caching, about constrained decoding, about handling many short requests that share a lot of context. So sometimes the model itself isn't that different, but the usage pattern forces us to adapt anyway.

And then the third dimension is the kernels. Every generation tends to come with some numerical trick, like new quantization formats or attention variants, and whether you can hit good performance really depends on whether the low-level kernels exist for your hardware. If they don't, you can get the model running in a week, but getting it running fast might take months.

So my rough mental model is: small adaptation if it's the same architecture family, medium if it changes memory or parallelism, large if it changes the whole shape of the workload. And in practice I'd say the industry has gotten better at the first two, but the third one keeps surprising us.

r001.rationale: The candidate says adaptation is small for a familiar architecture and that the cost jumps when the architecture changes structurally, clearly linking greater architectural change to more adaptation work.

astra-6.text:
I’d judge it by the gap between what the new model can do and what your application needs it to do. A new generation might perform better overall, but that doesn’t tell you how much work it will take to fit into your product.

So I’d start with representative tasks from the application and see where it succeeds and where it fails. Are the failures about following instructions, missing domain knowledge, or using tools correctly? Those point to different kinds of adaptation. Some may need a prompt change; others may need better context, changes to the workflow, or fine-tuning.

The key is to keep the evaluation consistent across generations. Otherwise, you’re judging by how impressive a few answers look, rather than whether the model reliably meets your requirements.

r001.rationale: The response links adaptation effort to the gap between model capabilities and application needs, but does not state that greater architectural changes require more adaptation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate what improves automatically with a stronger model from what still needs to be adapted for a specific task. I would start by running the new model on the same representative tasks, with as few changes as possible, and looking at where it fails. Does it misunderstand the task? Is it missing context? Or does it understand what to do but struggle to execute reliably?

Those are different problems. Sometimes you only need to adjust the prompt or the information you provide. Sometimes you need to change the workflow around the model. And sometimes you may need fine-tuning. So I wouldn’t judge the amount of adaptation just by how different the new model is. I’d judge it by the gap between its actual performance and what your application requires.

r001.rationale: The response judges adaptation by the gap between performance and application needs, and says not to judge it by how different the model is. It does not state that architectural changes increase adaptation work.
